title: Manuel Carlevaro
text:
After finishing high school in Paraná, I began my university studies, simultaneously pursuing two degrees: Electromechanical Engineering at the Universidad Tecnológica Nacional, and Bioengineering at the Universidad Nacional de Entre Ríos. But I really wanted to study physics, so in 1990 I moved to the city of Rosario.
I graduated with a Licentiate in Physics from the Universidad Nacional de Rosario in 1995, and then obtained my PhD from the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas of the Universidad Nacional de La Plata in 2002, thanks to a doctoral fellowship from CONICET.



While finishing my PhD, I began working as a researcher in the Agribusiness and Food Program of the Universidad de Buenos Aires (2001 – 2002), developing computational models of agrifood chains. Subsequently, I worked at the Nuclear Regulatory Authority (2003 – 2007) on projects related to the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, the analysis of environmental samples by gamma spectrometry, and the modeling and calibration of high-purity germanium detectors. In 2004, I also developed a simulation model of the honey export business of BOMARE S. A. Although the subjects were very different, the common thread was the same as in my current work: building computational models and using them to simulate and analyze scenarios.
In 2007, I joined CONICET as an Assistant Researcher at the Instituto de Física de Líquidos y Sistemas Biológicos (IFLySiB), which depends on CONICET and the Universidad Nacional de La Plata, where I currently work, but now as an Independent Researcher and head of the Statistical Mechanics of Liquids and Soft Condensed Matter group.
In 2009 and 2010, I held research stays at the Laboratory of Computational Biophysics and Molecular Modeling of the Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil), first with a fellowship from Brazil’s National Laboratory for Scientific Computing and then with a CONICET external postdoctoral fellowship, studying the interaction of integrins with their ligands through molecular modeling. At the Universidad Tecnológica Nacional, I led the Granular Materials Group of the Facultad Regional La Plata (2018 – 2025), and since 2025 I have directed the Centro de Investigación en Mecánica Experimental y Computacional.
As a teacher, I worked between 1993 and 1996 at the Universidad Nacional de Rosario (in the faculties of Engineering, Medicine, Veterinary Medicine, and Biochemistry and Pharmacy), and also at the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas of the Universidad Nacional de La Plata between 1997 and 2001. In 2005, I started as an Assistant Professor at the Facultad Regional Buenos Aires of the Universidad Tecnológica Nacional, teaching Physics II, and since 2018 I have been working as a Full Professor at the Facultad Regional La Plata of the same university, teaching undergraduate courses (currently Advanced Calculus) as well as graduate courses.

title: Research
text:
My work focuses on computational modeling and simulation of many-particle systems. The tools come from statistical mechanics: molecular dynamics, the discrete element method (DEM) and its coupling with computational fluid dynamics (CFD–DEM), Monte Carlo, liquid-state theory, genetic algorithms and neural networks. I apply them to problems at very different scales, from proteins and fluids in nanopores to grains flowing through an aperture and tissues made of thousands of cells.
Beyond academic research, I have taken part in collaborations and technological services with companies such as YPF Tecnología (Y-TEC), Mainero and BOMARE S. A.
The sections below summarize my current research lines, with a few representative papers. The full list is in Publications.



I study how granular materials flow, clog and transmit forces. These are out-of-equilibrium systems in which grain shape and friction determine the collective behavior. Using DEM simulations, I analyze clogging of grains passing through narrow apertures and how to reduce it by adding small, low-friction or magnetic particles; the discharge of silos with granular mixtures; the stick-slip dynamics of an intruder moving through a granular medium; the structure of force networks; and the use of granular materials to attenuate vibrations (particle dampers). Coupled with fluid dynamics (CFD–DEM), the same tools are applied to the transport and conductivity of proppants in fractures of unconventional reservoirs.
Frequent collaborators: L. A. Pugnaloni, L. Kondic, R. Kozlowski, J. E. S. Socolar, M. A. Madrid, M. Sánchez.

When a fluid is confined in pores or channels a few nanometers wide, its structure and transport differ from those of the bulk fluid. I study how granular materials flow, clog and transmit forces. These are out-of-equilibrium systems in which grain shape and friction determine the collective behavior. Using DEM simulations, I analyze clogging of grains passing through narrow apertures and how to reduce it by adding small, low-friction or magnetic particles; the discharge of silos with granular mixtures; the stick-slip dynamics of an intruder moving through a granular medium; the structure of force networks; and the use of granular materials to attenuate vibrations (particle dampers). Coupled with fluid dynamics (CFD–DEM), the same tools are applied to the transport and conductivity of proppants in fractures of unconventional reservoirs.
